column1: In the formal definition of a distributed system, what is the critical invariant regarding node state and communication?
column2: No shared state exists; node n_i can only influence node n_j by sending messages along a channel (n_i, n_j) ∈ C, possibly transitively through intermediate nodes.

column1: Per the CAP theorem (Gilbert & Lynch, 2002), since network partitions are unavoidable, what is the real architectural choice systems face?
column2: Between CP (sacrifice availability during partitions) and AP (sacrifice consistency during partitions) — partition tolerance itself is non-negotiable.

column1: Why does data locality become a first-class architectural concern in big data systems (quantify with the network vs. disk invariant)?
column2: Moving 1 TB over a 10 Gbps network takes ~800s, vs ~500s from local NVMe and ~5,000s from local HDD — the network is the bottleneck, so scheduling computation where data resides minimizes costly data movement.

column1: In a 1,000-node cluster with 99.9% per-node uptime, why must systems treat failure as the normal operating condition rather than an exception?
column2: The expected number of simultaneously failed nodes at any time is ~1, and the probability of at least one failure over 24 hours approaches certainty — failure is statistical, not exceptional.

column1: What is Spark's three-tier task locality preference order, and what mechanism governs relaxation between tiers?
column2: NODE_LOCAL > RACK_LOCAL > ANY; the scheduler waits a configurable `spark.locality.wait` duration at each tier before relaxing to the next, less-local tier.

column1: Contrast Spark's lineage-based recovery with Flink's checkpoint-based recovery in terms of cost tradeoffs.
column2: Lineage-based recovery (Spark RDDs) recomputes lost partitions by re-executing the transformation chain — cheap for narrow transforms (map/filter) but catastrophic for wide transforms (shuffles/joins). Checkpoint-based recovery (Flink) periodically snapshots full operator state to durable storage — fixed periodic overhead but bounded recovery cost regardless of transformation depth.

column1: What are the three notions of time that streaming systems must distinguish, per the Time Domain Problem?
column2: Event time (when the event occurred, embedded in payload), ingestion time (when the event entered the system), and processing time (when the system processes the event).

column1: What are the three invariants governing distributed storage design (durability, consistency, locality)?
column2: Durability: an acknowledged write survives N simultaneous failures via independent failure domains. Consistency: reads return the latest acknowledged write or a causally consistent value, tunable in strictness. Locality: data is placed physically close to the computation that processes it to minimize network I/O.

column1: Compare replication and erasure coding as fault-tolerance strategies in distributed storage.
column2: Replication stores K identical copies across K failure domains, with K× storage overhead and minimized read latency (any replica serves reads). Erasure coding achieves fault tolerance with lower storage overhead but at higher computational/reconstruction cost on failure.

column1: What does the source-coding theorem guarantee about Shannon entropy H(X) and compression, and why does this matter for key management?
column2: No lossless compression can represent X with fewer than H(X) bits per symbol on average — this is a hard information-theoretic lower bound. A 256-bit AES key with full entropy resists brute-force search provably, whereas human-chosen passwords may carry far fewer effective bits of entropy despite long byte length.

column1: What is the core architectural invariant of AEAD (e.g., AES-256-GCM) regarding ciphertext decryption?
column2: A ciphertext decrypts correctly if and only if both the key and the authentication tag match; any bit flip causes decryption to fail with overwhelming probability (1 − 2⁻¹²⁸), rather than silently producing corrupted plaintext.

column1: Why is BLAKE3 architecturally significant compared to SHA-256 for big-data integrity verification?
column2: BLAKE3 uses a Merkle tree construction that is natively parallelizable, achieving ~10 GB/s throughput versus SHA-256's ~0.5 GB/s without hardware acceleration, making it practical for integrity checks on petabyte-scale data blocks.
